title: Jews by choice
hook: converts, like Ruth, are fully Jewish; reminding them of their past is forbidden

segments.voice: Yesterday, minyan, and your line was fifteen million: a big number, counted with care, one face at a time. Did you picture a face inside a number? Today, some of those faces arrived by choosing. Day one thousand forty-six.

A dusty road out of Moab. Three widows walking. The oldest, Naomi, is going home to Bethlehem, and she turns to her two daughters-in-law and tells them to go back to their own mothers. One of them, Orpah, kisses her and goes, and the text doesn't blame her. The other, Ruth, holds on, and tells her: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Today is about people who say that sentence with their lives.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `ORPAH GOES HOME.` → `RUTH HOLDS ON.`

segments.voice: Jewish tradition reads Ruth as a convert, someone not born Jewish who chose to join the people and its God. Hebrew has a phrase for such a person: ger tzedek, a righteous convert. The word ger in the Torah means a stranger, someone who lives among you. The Torah is firm about the stranger: "The stranger that sojourneth with you shall be unto you as the home-born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The rabbis read that verse, among others, about converts. And the Mishnah sets down a rule about words that wound: to someone from a family of converts, you may not say, remember what your ancestors did. You don't bring up their past. You don't make them a guest in their own house. In Jewish law, once someone has converted, they are fully Jewish. Not almost. Not Jewish with a footnote. When a convert asked the medieval sage Maimonides whether he could say the words in the prayers, our God and God of our fathers, Maimonides answered yes: Abraham is his father too. And look how the book of Ruth ends. Ruth marries Boaz, and her great-grandson is David, the king. The family line of Israel's king runs through a woman from Moab who chose. Today, people convert within each of the Jewish movements, after study, usually before a rabbinic court, and often with immersion in a ritual bath. The movements differ on the details and on whose conversions they accept, and those differences are real. But the teaching the rabbis left is plain: a person who chose is not a lesser Jew. Fully Jewish.
screen: `GER TZEDEK: A RIGHTEOUS CONVERT.` · `LOVE THE STRANGER AS THYSELF.` · `DON'T BRING UP THEIR PAST.` · `RUTH'S GREAT-GRANDSON, DAVID.` · then, large: `FULLY JEWISH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: welcome someone who chose. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind someone who joined a group you belong to rather than being born into it: a new neighbor, an in-law, a colleague, someone who came to your faith or your country. Notice whether, somewhere in you, they are still the new one. Then picture saying something that makes it plain they belong, without a word about where they came from. Hold that until the bell, and if you can, say it to them this week. The bell holds the time.
Ger tzedek. A righteous convert, someone who chose to join the Jewish people, and who, like Ruth, is fully Jewish, with a past no one may throw at them. Today's word.
Your line: fully jewish. Today, treat one newcomer anywhere as if they'd always been there. Day one thousand forty-six.

howItsDone: Conversion to Judaism involves study with a rabbi and usually appearing before a rabbinic court, and often immersion in a mikveh; movements differ in their requirements, and Jewish law forbids reminding a convert of their past.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts; superlatives about Ruth's words and David cut.
'The rabbis read that verse, among others, about converts': the rabbinic reading of ger as convert; please confirm phrasing.
Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 paraphrased; Maimonides' letter to Obadiah paraphrased (not quoted). Please confirm.

'People convert in every Jewish movement, after study, usually before a rabbinic court, and often with immersion': please confirm as a fair general description; movements differ on requirements and mutual recognition, stated without ranking.
Ruth 1:16 and Leviticus 19:34: please confirm the JPS 1917 wording of the quoted portions.

Editor pass: the teach no longer says the Mishnah's rule was 'drawn from' Leviticus 19:34 (Bava Metzia 4:10 does not derive it from that verse; the Gemara links the topic to Exodus 22:20), and the rule is now stated as the Mishnah gives it, about someone from a family of converts (teach and myth); cut 'has been carried down ever since'; softened 'in every Jewish movement' and 'inside each community the teaching is the same'.

Audit: 'fully Jewish' attributed to Jewish law rather than the narrator; 'with a rabbinic court' softened to 'usually before a rabbinic court' (teach and howItsDone), since practice differs across movements.
